statement: In the UK mephedrone scare of 2009–2010, several deaths that online news linked to mephedrone were later reported not to have been caused by it, including the deaths most linked to it online; the evidence is one study of online news whose later toxicology is second-hand (as later reported, not taken from coroners' records), so its figures are illustrative. Searching Google News from 26 November 2009 to one year after the ban (enforced on 16 April 2010), the author found 18 named people whose deaths online news linked to mephedrone; suicides and violent or accidental deaths were left out, and their number is not given. Later reports said that mephedrone was not found in 4, including two young men in Scunthorpe, whose names were linked to mephedrone on about 9,060 and 8,730 web pages by June 2011 (more than any other case), who were reported a month after the ban not to have taken mephedrone, and whose inquest in 2011 found that they died from alcohol combined with methadone; that it was found but was not a factor in 4; and that it was a factor in 7, six of them with other drugs or illnesses also alleged. For 3 there was no later toxicology note, and the first death linked to mephedrone, of a 14-year-old girl in November 2009, was reported in local news within a month as due to natural causes (pneumonia after a streptococcal infection), yet went on being named as a mephedrone death in local, national and international news for months. The author reads the volume of news as showing that reports confirming that mephedrone was not responsible were far fewer than the earlier reports suggesting that it was. In screenshots of relative Google search indices without absolute numbers, searches for 'mephedrone' rose around the most-reported deaths and fell after the ban, and searches for 'mephedrone buy' rose far more after the Scunthorpe deaths than after the first death (no 'mephedrone buy' data are shown after 24 March 2010). The author reads this as suggesting a 'boomerang effect', news of drug deaths raising interest in the drug, including in buying it, while conceding that a search is not a purchase and that the data show neither how many people searched nor why; in the editors' reading, timing in screenshots cannot show that the news made people seek or use the drug (Forsyth, 2012). For comparison, the paper cites official statistics recording 6 drug-related deaths involving mephedrone, confirmed by toxicology, among 2,747 drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 2010, 2 of them with mephedrone as the only drug found, without giving the definition used (as cited by Forsyth, 2012). The 18 deaths are the media's selection, not a count of deaths involving mephedrone, and the outcome of each is as later reported, not taken from coroners' records; how many deaths blamed on mephedrone were confirmed in national registers is in the answer on confirmed mephedrone deaths. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right? Not always. In 2009 and 2010, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone. Later reports said mephedrone was not found in 4 of them, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses. The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone, and the first death in the news was reported as natural causes within a month. Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news. The author thinks the news raised interest in the drug, but search data cannot show that the news made people use it. This comes from one study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.
population: Deaths of named people that UK online news linked to mephedrone between November 2009 and about April 2011 (18; suicides and violent or accidental deaths excluded)
exposure: Online news reports attributing a death to mephedrone
comparator: Mephedrone's role as later reported in the press from inquests (not detected, detected but not a factor, a factor)
outcome: Whether mephedrone was later reported to have caused the deaths linked to it in the news; relative online search interest around the reports
magnitude: Forsyth (2012), 18 named deaths linked to mephedrone in online news (26 November 2009 to about April 2011; suicides and violent or accidental deaths excluded, number not given). Later reports (second-hand): not detected 4; detected, not a factor 4; detected and a factor 7 (6 with other drugs or conditions alleged); no toxicology note 3 (one reported as natural causes); editors' tally of Table 1 notes. Most-linked cases: 9,060 and 8,730 web pages (Scunthorpe; alcohol and methadone at inquest). Cited from ONS: 6 toxicologically confirmed mephedrone-related deaths among 2,747 drug-related deaths, England and Wales, 2010; mephedrone the only drug in 2. Search data are relative indices without absolute numbers, with no 'mephedrone buy' data after 24 March 2010.

evidence.extracted: Google News was used to read in date order all online news about mephedrone from 26/11/09 until one year after the ban and to identify all UK mephedrone deaths reported online; Google Advanced Search counted web pages for each death ('Mephedrone AND [name]'); Google Trends and Insights gave search volume for 'mephedrone' and 'mephedrone buy'. Limitations stated: one search engine; Google News uses sources it selects (it says about 4500 English-language news sites); Trends values are normalised to the highest volume, so they give relative, not absolute, numbers.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the claim concerns online news about these deaths in one scare, as the study does.

grade.reasoning: A case series of deaths named in the news, starting low as observational evidence; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: very low. The claim rests only on this case series, whose toxicology is second-hand (as later reported, not from records), so it stays at draft and says its figures are illustrative (brief; METHODS §6.3). The search-interest findings are co-occurrence in screenshots and are reported as not showing cause, as the author concedes, although he reads them as suggesting that news of the deaths raised interest in the drug. Status single study; the project's reading list found no other study comparing news reports of individual drug deaths with later inquest or toxicology findings. The national register series of deaths blamed on mephedrone is a separate answer.

statement: By 31 October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK, Channel Islands and Isle of Man had been alleged to be associated with mephedrone. Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25 (19.5%, editors’ calculation), and 13 results were pending. The Results describe 90 as positive, 69 with concluded inquests, and 62 with forms received and analysed (Schifano et al., 2012). This flow has an exception: Table 2 says one of the 62 died in hospital three weeks after taking mephedrone and had none found after death. The paper mentions ante-mortem findings collectively but does not give this person’s individual confirmation evidence. A negative test after death does not establish no earlier exposure. The cases came from the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths, internet searches of toxicology and news sites, and a toxicology group. Coroners and Scottish procurators fiscal supplied records; media reports sometimes filled gaps. The register admits deaths with a directly implicated psychoactive substance, a history of dependence or misuse, or a controlled drug present after death. Presence of mephedrone itself could meet the last criterion only after its classification, which the paper dates to spring 2010; the entry criterion for each death is not stated (editors’ reading; Schifano et al., 2012). Mephedrone was the only substance identified in 8 of 62. The remaining 54 (62−8, editors’ calculation) were outside that only-substance group; this subtraction does not establish an individual co-detection result for the post-mortem-negative exception. Alcohol 26, other stimulants 22 and hypnotics or sedatives 22 were the most common other categories. Categories overlap and do not identify which substance caused a death. Mephedrone was formally named in the recorded cause in 36, on its own in 18. Who made those causal decisions and what evidence or rules they used are unstated (Schifano et al., 2012). The authors separately grouped 26 deaths as acute drug toxicity, 18 as self-inflicted harm, 6 as risky behaviour, 5 as collapse at a party, 5 as delayed hospital deaths and 2 as risky sexual activity. Those circumstance groups differ from the legal verdicts: 35 accident or misadventure, 11 suicide, 8 open, 5 drug misuse, and 1 each homicide, natural causes and narrative. The paper does not reconcile 18 self-inflicted deaths with 11 suicide verdicts; neither classification establishes that mephedrone caused self-harm (Schifano et al., 2012). The authors explicitly distinguish detection from causation and caution that failure to detect mephedrone may reflect test limitations. They regard the count as a minimum because some positive cases awaited inquest, geographical reporting was incomplete and tests varied. About 95% of coroners’ areas in England and Wales reported regularly; this is not 95% completeness of deaths across the UK. Untested or unalleged deaths could also be missed (editors’ inference, not a measured source finding). The Discussion names blood for the quantified levels, but blood type, sampling site and time, laboratory methods and panels are not described. With no count of use, this series supplies no death rate. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How many deaths linked to mephedrone were confirmed? By October 2011, 128 deaths had been alleged in the UK and nearby islands. Tests after death found no mephedrone in 25, and 13 results were pending. Of 62 deaths analysed, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death; the paper does not explain their individual earlier test evidence. Being counted as confirmed did not mean mephedrone caused the death. The authors also say tests and reporting could miss deaths. This study cannot give a death rate.
population: 128 deaths alleged by 31 October 2011 in the UK, Channel Islands and Isle of Man; 62 analysed after concluded inquests and receipt of register forms, with one post-mortem-negative delayed hospital death despite the Results’ positive-test definition
exposure: Alleged mephedrone exposure and recorded toxicology; the individual confirmation evidence for one post-mortem-negative delayed death is unstated
comparator: None: no deaths without mephedrone, no deaths from other causes and no count of people using mephedrone
outcome: Whether mephedrone was found after death; whether it was named in the recorded cause of death; other substances found; circumstances and verdicts
magnitude: 128 alleged: 25 post-mortem-negative, 13 pending, 90 described as positive; 69 concluded inquests; 62 analysed, including the Table 2 post-mortem-negative exception. Editors’ calculations: 25/128=19.5%, 25/115 with results=21.7%, 8/62 only-substance=12.9%, 36/62 named-in-cause=58.1%, outside only-substance group 54=62−8 (not individual co-detection evidence for the negative exception). Named alone in recorded cause 18. Other substances: alcohol 26, stimulants 22, hypnotics/sedatives 22, opioids 13, piperazines 13, other cathinones 13. Author circumstance groups 26/18/6/5/5/2 differ from legal verdicts 35/11/8/5/1/1/1. No use denominator or printed intervals.

evidence.extracted: Sources and case definition: np-SAD has received coroners' information on drug-related deaths in the UK, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man since 1997 (and since 2004 from the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency and the General Register Office for Northern Ireland); most (95%) coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly, so the counts are a minimum. A death is recorded if a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, there was a history of dependence or drug misuse, or controlled drugs were present after death. Further cases came from internet searches of toxicological, newspaper and media websites and from the London Toxicology Group; media reports supplemented the data form where coroners' files could not be accessed; forms received by 31 October 2011 were analysed.
